extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers of classical mechanics, astronomy, and mathematical physics (readers of Newton's Principia)
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of propositions and corollaries from Newton's Principia giving precise mathematical statements about gravitational attraction (inverse-square law), the behaviour of spherical bodies, and perturbative effects in multi-body systems; includes proofs and explanatory scholia. Useful for deriving how distributed masses act on interior and exterior points and for predicting orbital perturbations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 7: Apsidal line progression/regression
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellipse's axis (line of apsides) sometimes advances and sometimes regresses in angular motion, but on the whole it advances; in each revolution the apsidal line is carried forward by the net excess of progression. The perturbing force on P composes from LM and the centripetal force by S; LM increases with PS distance nearly in same ratio as distance, KL decreases in the duplicate ratio, so their sum decreases in less than the duplicate ratio and causes regression; in conjunction & opposition the resulting difference causes progression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how composition of perturbing forces (LM, KL) and their distance dependence determine whether the apsidal line advances or retreats; shows conjunctions tend to produce forward (prograde) motion of the apsides while quadratures tend to cause regression. Use to predict apsidal motion from relative phasing of perturbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 8: Location of maximal apsidal advance/regress
rubrics_metrics.description: Apsidal progression or regression depends on the deviation of the centripetal force from an inverse-square law across the orbit; the maximum effect occurs where the ratio of the centripetal force at apse to that at periapse departs most from the inverse-square ratio. Apsides in their syzygies (conjunction/opposition) will progress faster; in their quadratures they recede more slowly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to locate where along the orbit the change of apsidal line is largest: syzygies give strongest advance, quadratures weaker regression; long durations amplify the inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 9: Effect of incremental centripetal force on eccentricity
rubrics_metrics.description: If a body moving under a force proportionate to inverse-square of distance receives, on descent from apse to periapse, a continual increment of an additional force that increases by more than the duplicate ratio of distance diminution, then the orbit becomes more interior and eccentricity increases; conversely, if the incremental change per revolution diminishes, eccentricity decreases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relates how systematic incremental increases or decreases of a perturbing centripetal component each revolution change orbital eccentricity; used to infer whether perturbations will grow or damp eccentricity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 10: Latitude (inclination) perturbations from tangential/normal components
rubrics_metrics.description: Forces NM and ML (components of perturbing forces) do not disturb latitude when acting in the orbital plane; NM at nodes in syzygies also acts in the plane and doesn't perturb latitude. In quadratures NM most perturbs latitude causing the body P to be drawn out of its orbital plane, modifying the inclination as P moves from quadrature to syzygy and back.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predicts how nodal and quadrature alignments of the perturbing body change orbital inclination: minima of inclination occur at syzygies, maxima at certain octants depending on node placement. Useful for tidal/obliquity reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 11: Nodal motion (regression/advance) depending on node location
rubrics_metrics.description: When nodes are in quadrature the node locations perpetually recede (regress) as P moves from node through conjunction to the next node; in syzygies (where latitude motion is unperturbed) nodes are stationary; in intermediate positions nodes recede more slowly and thus appear retrograde or stationary each revolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives rule for nodal precession: nodes at quadrature steadily regress, at syzygies remain fixed; intermediate nodes show intermediate behavior. Use to infer node evolution from phasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 12: Errors larger in conjunction than opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: All the described errors (apsidal, nodal, inclination, eccentricity perturbations) are a little greater in conjunction than in opposition, owing to the larger forces NM & ML generated in conjunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple comparative rule: conjunction produces stronger perturbations than opposition because of larger generated perturbing components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 13: Independence of corollaries from magnitude of Q under certain configuration
rubrics_metrics.description: The above corollaries hold regardless of the magnitude of body Q provided Q is large enough that S and P revolve about it; increasing Q (and hence its centripetal force) makes the errors produced (for equal distances) larger in that case than when Q revolves around the S–P system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows the qualitative laws are scale-invariant as to Q's magnitude, but magnitudes of effects scale with Q; indicates when one may treat results as general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 14: Scaling of NM and ML and their effects for distant Q
rubrics_metrics.description: When Q is distant, the forces NM, ML are approximately QK × (PS/QS) (i.e. proportional to Q's absolute force and to PS/QS), so all the effects discussed scale, for fixed S–P system, approximately as the product of Q's absolute force and the inverse cube of QS. If Q's mass is proportional to its absolute force, NM, ML and their effects scale as the cube of the apparent diameter of the distant body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives quantitative scaling: perturbation amplitudes ∝ (Q_force) × (1/QS^3); temporal scaling is reciprocal to the square of the periodic time. Useful for estimating magnitudes of perturbations from distant bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 15: Proportionality of errors with geometric/temporal scaling
rubrics_metrics.description: If orbit shapes and mutual inclinations remain but sizes, masses, forces and distances scale, the effects scale proportionally: linear errors scale as orbital diameters, angular errors as before, and times scale as orbital periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides scaling laws for transferring computed errors/times between geometrically similar systems with scaled masses or sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 16: Predicting errors across systems from one case
rubrics_metrics.description: Given orbit forms & inclinations, and any changes of bodies' magnitudes, forces & distances, one can derive errors and their times in one case from those in another: NM, ML (other things equal) are as radius SP, and their periodic effects are as the forces times the square of the periodic times. Angular errors of P about S in each revolution are approximately proportional to the square of P's period and inversely to the square of S's period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives method to transform computed perturbations from one system to another using proportionalities with radii and period-squared factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 17: Relation between mediating forces and orbital periods
rubrics_metrics.description: The mean force LM per radius PS is to the mean force QK or QN (exposed through QS) as PS to QS. The mean force LM that retains P about S is in the duplicated ratio of the periodic times; given periods and PS, LM (and approximately MN) are determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a way to relate mean perturbing forces to observable distances and periods—useful for inferring perturbing magnitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 18: Behaviour of contiguous fluid annuli under perturbation
rubrics_metrics.description: If many fluid bodies at equal distances around S coalesce into a circular annulus concentric with S, each annulus element moves according to the same law as body P: they approach S and move faster in conjunctions & oppositions than in quadratures. The ring's nodes (intersections with Q or S orbital plane) are stationary in syzygies and move fastest in quadratures; the annulus' inclination and axis oscillate with each revolution, returning to original position except for nodal precession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains tidal/annular fluid response to perturbing body Q; applies to ring dynamics and tidal bulges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 19: Tidal flow on a rotating globe under perturbation
rubrics_metrics.description: If a sphere S contains water in a circumferential trench and rotates uniformly, the water will be alternately accelerated and retarded by Q's uneven attraction: water nearer Q is more attracted than farther water, producing flows that lead to rise toward syzygies and fall toward quadratures — i.e., tides faster/slower than the globe surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a mechanical explanation for tide-like flow produced by an external attracting body; shows removal of Q eliminates that flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 20: Effect of rigid annulus on globe's motion and nodal precession
rubrics_metrics.description: If the annulus is rigidly attached to the globe, the flowing motion ceases but oscillation of inclination and nodal precession remain. A globe sharing axis and contact with the annulus will receive and retain impressed motions, oscillate, and cause nodal regression/advance depending on configuration; maxima/minima of inclination occur at specified orbital phasings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes gyroscopic response and persistence of impressed oscillatory motions when fluid replaced by rigid coupling; useful for modeling coupled solid-fluid rotational dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 21: Excess equatorial matter causes nodal regression
rubrics_metrics.description: An excess of mass near the equator causes nodal regression; increasing equatorial surplus increases regression, decreasing it decreases regression; removing equatorial surplus can eliminate regression and cause nodes to advance instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connects mass distribution (equatorial bulge) to nodal precession direction and magnitude; applicable to planetary oblateness effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 22: Inferring globe constitution from nodal motion
rubrics_metrics.description: From the direction of nodal motion one can deduce mass distribution: if a globe keeps poles constant and nodes move forward, equatorial surplus exists; if nodes move backward, equator is surplused. A homogeneous, perfectly spherical globe keeps a fixed axis under impulses; adding or redistributing mass leads to pole wandering and nodal behavior described earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives diagnostic: observe nodal/progression behavior to infer internal/external mass asymmetries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition LXVII (Theorem XXVII): Use of common center of gravity reduces perturbation
rubrics_metrics.description: An external body Q revolving about the common center of gravity C of two interior bodies P and S, with radii drawn to C, describes areas more proportional to times and describes an orbit closer to an ellipse with umbilic at C than when radii are drawn to the inner larger body S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule: when modeling motion of an external perturber Q in a system of two inner masses, use radii to the common centre of gravity for more nearly Keplerian (area-law/elliptic) description; minimizes perturbation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition LXVIII (Theorem XXVIII): Effect of internal body's own motion on perturbation
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar to LXVII: If the inner larger body S is moved/acted upon comparably to other effects, the orbit of the exterior Q about common centre C will have areas more proportional to times and be more nearly elliptic when referenced to C than when referenced to S; minimal perturbation occurs when the common centre is at rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reinforces that treating motion relative to the common centre of gravity yields the least perturbed (most Keplerian) motion for the external body; perturbations increase when the internal bodies' common centre moves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition LXIX (Theorem XXIX): Absolute attracting forces proportional to bodies (mass)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a system of many bodies A, B, C, D..., if A attracts all others with accelerative forces inversely proportional to squares of distance from A, and B likewise attracts all others in the same way, then the absolute attracting forces of A and B on each other are to one another as the bodies A and B themselves (i.e., as their masses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fundamental derivation that links the accelerative (field) attractions to absolute attraction (force) and thereby gives proportionality of attracting forces to the magnitudes (masses) of bodies; Q.E.D. — forms a basis for mass concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 1 to LXIX: Absolute forces scale with bodies when each attracts others
rubrics_metrics.description: If each member of a system attracts all others by accelerative forces ~1/(distance^2), then the absolute forces of the bodies on one another are proportional to the bodies themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate consequence: masses are proportional to their absolute gravitational powers when accelerations satisfy inverse-square.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 2 to LXIX: Extension to general distance laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The same argument holds if accelerative attractions are any common law (direct or inverse power) of distances from the attracting body (i.e., a common functional dependence). In that case absolute attracting forces are still proportional to the bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalizes LXIX beyond inverse-square to any common distance-dependence law among the bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 3 to LXIX: Orbits & area-law for small bodies about a large one
rubrics_metrics.description: In a system where smaller bodies revolve about a large one on ellipses with common umbilic at the large body's centre and areas proportional to times, their absolute attracting forces are (accurately or approximately) proportional to the bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connects observational orbital regularities (Keplerian behavior) to deducing proportionality of absolute force to mass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium: Modeling attraction by summing particle contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy between centripetal forces and central bodies: where attraction arises from distributed parts (as in magnetics) assign to each particle a proper force and sum them. 'Attraction' is used generally for any tendency of bodies toward one another whether by direct action, emitted spirits, ether, air, or other media. In mathematics one first determines quantitative relations from given conditions, then compares with phenomena to decide the physical nature of the forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological guidance: treat distributed bodies by assigning elemental attractions and summing; separate the mathematical deduction of consequences from physical interpretation of causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition LXX (Theorem XXX): Hollow spherical shell exerts no net internal attraction
rubrics_metrics.description: If equal centripetal forces tending from each point of a spherical surface act on an interior body and decrease as the duplicate ratio (inverse square) of the distances from those points, then the resultant attraction on an interior particle is zero (no net attraction toward any direction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic shell theorem: for inverse-square pointwise attraction distributed uniformly over a thin spherical shell, interior forces cancel exactly. Proof uses pairing of symmetric surface elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition LXXI (Theorem XXXI): Spherical shell attracts external point as if mass at centre
rubrics_metrics.description: For equal spherical surface elements AHKB and ahkb with common centres and equal diameters, a point P exterior on the diameter is attracted by the shell with a force proportional to the inverse square of its distance from the shell's centre — i.e., the shell attracts as if all its force concentrated at centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Another part of the shell theorem: externally, a spherical shell behaves as though its mass were concentrated at its centre, yielding inverse-square dependence with centre distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition LXXII (Theorem XXXII): Force proportional to semi-diameter under given ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: If equal centripetal forces decreasing as inverse square tend from each point of a sphere, and the ratio of the sphere's diameter to the distance of the point from its centre is given, then the force by which the particle is attracted will be proportional to the semi-diameter (radius) of the sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to compare attraction magnitudes between spheres when distances scale with diameters; yields proportionality relations for forces when geometrical similarity and distance ratios are specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollaries to LXXII: Equal periods ⇄ proportional distances/diameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Corollary 1: If particles in circles about spheres of equal attracting matter at distances proportional to sphere diameters move, their periodic times are equal. Corollary 2: Conversely, equal periodic times imply distances proportional to diameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives relationships between orbital periods and geometrical scaling of sphere sizes and orbital radii in contexts where attractions scale with sphere radii.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition LXXIII (Theorem XXXIII): Force inside a homogeneous sphere is proportional to distance from centre
rubrics_metrics.description: If equal centripetal forces that decrease as inverse square of distance act from each point of a given sphere, then a particle inside that sphere is attracted toward the centre with a force proportional to its distance from the centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key result: inside a homogeneous sphere (summed inverse-square contributions) the net attraction behaves like Hooke's law (linear restoring force ∝ r). Use for deriving planetary interior dynamics and small oscillations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium on infinitesimal shells/particles
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarifies that the 'surfaces' and 'points' used in proofs are to be understood in the infinitesimal sense: spheres are composed of infinitely many vanishingly thin shells or particles; the reasoning proceeds by letting shell thickness → 0 and particle size → 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological note on treating continuous bodies via infinitesimal decomposition — justification for applying earlier shell results to solid spheres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition LXXIV (Theorem XXXIV): Solid sphere attracts external point with inverse-square law
rubrics_metrics.description: A solid sphere composed of attracting particles (each exerting inverse-square forces) attracts an external point such that the total attraction is reciprocally proportional to the square of the distance from the sphere's centre (i.e., as if all mass concentrated at centre).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalization: any homogeneous solid sphere attracts external bodies as if its mass were at the centre (shell theorem extension to solid sphere via concentric shells).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollaries to LXXIV: Attraction scales with spheres and surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Corollary 1: At equal distances from centres of homogeneous spheres, attractions are proportional to the spheres themselves (volumes). Corollary 2: For arbitrary distances, attractions are proportional to sphere content applied to inverse-square of distance. Corollary 3: If a homogeneous sphere attracts with inverse-square law and is composed of attracting particles, then the particle-level force must itself decay as inverse-square.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizes consequences for proportional comparisons of attractions between spheres and links microscopic decay law to macroscopic inverse-square behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition LXXV (Theorem XXXV): Similar spheres attract as point masses at centers
rubrics_metrics.description: If equal centripetal forces decreasing as inverse-square act from each point of a sphere, any other similar sphere is attracted reciprocally as the square of centre distances — i.e., spheres attract each other as if their masses concentrated at their centres with inverse-square dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes mutual attraction of spheres as though concentrated at centres; corollaries explain proportionality to volumes (contents) and the doubling of effect when both attract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollaries to LXXV: Mutual attraction and orbit consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Corollary 1: Attraction between homogeneous spheres applied at equal centre-distances is as the spheres (volumes). Corollary 2: Same holds if the attracted sphere also attracts. Corollary 3: Results about motion about conic-section centres apply when spheres replace point masses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how sphere–sphere attractions reproduce point-mass results for orbital motion; facilitates using sphere models in celestial mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition LXXVI (Theorem XXXVI): Concentric varying-density spheres still attract as inverse-square
rubrics_metrics.description: If spheres differ in radial density (concentric similar shells whose densities vary with radius but at any given distance from centre shells are similar), and the pointwise attractive force of each particle decays as inverse-square, then the total attraction of one such sphere on another is reciprocally proportional to the square of the distance between their centres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalizes earlier shell/sphere results to radially non-homogeneous spheres composed of concentric similar shells; shows preservation of inverse-square centre-to-centre law for total attraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollaries to LXXVI: Multiple consequences on periods, scaling, and motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Corollaries 1–8: include (1) mutual singular attractions among similar spheres scale as the spheres' contents at equal centre-distances; (2) for unequal distances apply content×(1/dist^2); (3) motional weights/gravities follow multiplicative product of contents at equal distances; (4) similar for unequal distances; (5) mutual attraction doubling if both act; (6) if such spheres revolve about others with center-distances proportional to resting diameters, periodic times are equal; (7) conversely periodic equality implies proportional distances; (8) all previous results about conic-section motions hold when attracting bodies are spheres of described form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collects practical consequences for orbital periods, scaling laws, and replacement of point masses by spheres (even with radial density variation) in gravitational calculations.
